We have mass spec data: m/z 183.04509 (intensity 100) likely molecular ion. That mass corresponds to formula? Let's compute approximate mass: C10H11ClO? Let's calculate: C10 = 120.0, H11 = 11.088, Cl = 35.45, O = 15.999 => total ~182.537. Actually monoisotopic mass: C (12.0000) *10 = 120.000, H (1.007825)*11 = 11.085, Cl (35.45? monoisotopic 35.45? Actually 35Cl = 34.96885), O (15.99491). Sum = 120 + 11.085 + 34.969 + 15.995 = 181. +? Let's compute: 120 + 11.085 = 131.085; +34.969 = 166.054; +15.995 = 182.049. That's close to 183.045 observed, maybe includes proton? Actually m/z 183.045 likely [M+H]+? If proton added, neutral mass ~182.045. That matches C10H10ClO? Let's compute C10H10ClO neutral: C10=120, H10=10.078, Cl=34.969, O=15.995 => total 180. +? 120+10.078=130.078; +34.969=165.047; +15.995=181.042. Add proton 1.007 => 182.049. Not 183.045. Maybe it's [M+Na]+? Na 22.99 gives 203. So not.

Maybe formula C9H9ClO? C9=108, H9=9.07, Cl=34.969, O=15.995 => total 167. +? 108+9.07=117.07; +34.969=152.039; +15.995=168.034. +H =169.041. Not.

Let's compute exact monoisotopic mass for C10H11ClO: 120 + 11.085 =131.085; +34.969=166.054; +15.995=182.049. Add proton =183.056. Observed 183.045, close (difference 0.011). Could be measurement error. So likely molecular ion [M+H]+ of C10H11ClO. So neutral formula C10H10ClO? Wait neutral would be C10H10ClO (since proton added). But we got C10H11ClO neutral mass 182.049, proton gives 183.056. Observed 183.045, close. So neutral formula likely C10H10ClO? Let's compute monoisotopic mass of C10H10ClO: H10 mass 10.078, sum = 120+10.078=130.078; +34.969=165.047; +15.995=181.042. +H =182.049. Not match. So C10H11ClO neutral mass 182.049, plus H =183.056. Observed 183.045, difference 0.011 (maybe due to using average mass). So plausible.

Thus formula C10H11ClO. Need SMILES. Could be chlorophenylacetone? Let's think: C10H11ClO suggests 10 carbons, 1 oxygen, 1 chlorine, 11 hydrogens. DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 = 10 - 11/2 +1 = 10 -5.5 +1 =5.5? Actually DBE formula: DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 +1 (halogens count as H). So treat Cl as H. So effective H = 11+1=12. DBE = 10 -12/2 +1 =10 -6 +1 =5. So 5 degrees unsaturation. With one O (likely carbonyl or alcohol). 5 DBE suggests aromatic ring (4 DBE) plus one extra double bond or ring. So likely a chlorobenzene derivative with carbonyl side chain (e.g., 4-chlorobenzaldehyde C7H5ClO? that's C7H5ClO, not enough C). Need 10 carbons: maybe chlorobenzyl acetone (C9?). Let's enumerate: phenyl (C6H5) plus Cl substituent adds Cl, plus carbonyl side chain maybe CH2COCH3? That's C5H7O? Actually CH2COCH3 = C3H5O? Wait CH2-CO-CH3: C3H5O? CH2 (CH2) = C1H2, CO = C1O1, CH3 = C1H3 => total C3H5O. Add to phenyl (C6H4 after substitution) gives C9H9O plus Cl = C9H9ClO. Not enough C.

We need C10. Maybe phenyl with Cl and ethyl ketone: phenyl-CO-CH2CH3? That's acetophenone with Cl on ring: C8H7O + Cl? Actually acetophenone C8H8O? Wait acetophenone: C8H8O? Actually phenyl (C6H5) + COCH3 (C2H3O) = C8H8O. Add Cl substituent on ring gives C8H7ClO? plus extra carbon? Not.

Maybe chlorobenzyl alcohol with extra carbon: C7H7ClO? Not.

Let's consider possible structure: 4-chlorobenzaldehyde (C7H5ClO). Not.

Maybe 2-chlorophenylacetonitrile? Contains N.

We have only O, no N.

Could be a chlorinated phenyl ether? e.g., chlorophenyl methyl ether (C7H7ClO). Not.

C10 suggests maybe a benzene ring (6 C) plus a side chain of 4 carbons containing carbonyl and chlorine maybe? But chlorine likely on aromatic.

Consider 4-chlorobenzyl acetate: C9H9ClO2 (has two O). Not.

Maybe 4-chlorobenzyl methyl ketone: C9H9ClO? Actually phenyl-CH2-CO-CH3: phenyl (C6H5) + CH2 (C1H2) + CO (C1O1) + CH3 (C1H3) = C9H10O. Add Cl on ring gives C9H9ClO. Not enough C.

We need C10, so maybe phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3? That's phenyl (C6H5) + CH2CH2 (C2H4) + COCH3 (C2H3O) = C10H12O. Add Cl on ring gives C10H11ClO. Yes! So structure: 4-chlorophenylpropyl methyl ketone? Actually chain: phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3 is phenylbutanone? Wait phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3 is 3-phenyl-2-butanone? Let's name: 1-phenyl-2-butanone? Actually carbonyl at position 2 of butanone attached to phenyl at carbon 1: phenyl-CO-CH2-CH3 is acetophenone. But we have phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3: that's phenylpropyl methyl ketone, also called 1-phenyl-1-propanone? No.

Better: 4-chlorophenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3 (para-chlorophenyl propanone). SMILES: Clc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)C? Wait chain: phenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3: SMILES: c1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)C. Add Cl at para: Clc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)C. That is C10H11ClO? Let's count: aromatic ring C6H4Cl (since one H replaced by Cl). Then side chain: CH2-CH2-CO-CH3 = C4H7O? Actually CH2 (C1H2) + CH2 (C1H2) + CO (C1O1) + CH3 (C1H3) = C4H7O. Combine: C6+4=10 C. H: aromatic H count: ring originally C6H5, but one H replaced by Cl, so H4. Add side chain H7 => total H11. O1, Cl1. Yes matches formula.

Thus SMILES: Clc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)C. Need correct aromatic notation: "Clc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)C". Could also be "Clc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)C". Validate.

We should validate SMILES.
